entries.title: Aïoli and the French rémoulade
entries.summary: Aïoli is the garlic sauce of Provence: garlic pounded with salt, olive oil worked in, usually with a yolk. The French rémoulade is mayonnaise with mustard, gherkins, capers, herbs and anchovy. Rouille, tartare and gribiche complete the family.
entries.guest: Aïoli is the garlic and olive oil sauce of Provence. Our Crawfish Meat Pies come with a chive rémoulade for dipping: cool, tangy and herby against the hot pastry.

paras: Aïoli and the French rémoulade are two pillars of the cold kitchen, each with a family around it. Aïoli, said eye-OH-lee, is the garlic sauce of Provence, and its name joins the Provençal words for garlic and oil. At its oldest it is nothing more: garlic pounded to a paste with coarse salt in a mortar, olive oil worked in drop by drop until it holds. Most kitchens now add an egg yolk, which makes it far steadier, so in practice it is a garlic mayonnaise made with olive oil.

In Provence, le grand aïoli is a whole meal built around the sauce: poached salt cod, boiled vegetables and hard-boiled eggs, all dipped in one big bowl. The French rémoulade, said REM-uh-lahd, is mayonnaise finished with mustard, chopped gherkins (small, sour pickled cucumbers), capers, herbs and a little anchovy: white, sharp and herby, for cold meats, fried fish and seafood.

For aïoli, pound 4 to 6 cloves of garlic with a good pinch of coarse salt to a smooth, sticky paste, pulling out any green shoot, which tastes harsh. Stir in one yolk and a few drops of water or lemon juice. Then mount it, meaning beat in the oil until the sauce thickens: about 250 ml (1 cup) of olive oil, a few drops at a time at first, then in a thin thread once it turns glossy. A peppery extra virgin oil can turn bitter beaten hard in a blender, so many cooks use half mild olive oil, or work by hand.

For the French rémoulade, start from a mayonnaise made with a neutral oil. To 250 ml (1 cup) of it add 1 tsp (5 ml) of Dijon mustard, 1 tbsp (15 ml) each of finely chopped gherkins and capers, squeezed dry in a cloth, 1 tbsp (15 ml) of chopped parsley, chervil and tarragon, and one anchovy fillet crushed to a paste. Rest it for half an hour and taste it cold.

Rouille, said roo-EE, French for rust, is aïoli's red cousin: garlic, chilli and a pinch of saffron pounded with bread soaked in fish broth, then mounted with olive oil, often with a yolk. It is spread on toasted bread and floated on bouillabaisse, the fish stew of Marseille.

Tartare and gribiche are the egg sauces. The classical French tartare was mounted not on raw yolks but on hard-boiled yolks pounded smooth, and finished with chives; most kitchens now make it as mayonnaise with gherkins, capers and herbs. Gribiche, said gree-BEESH, crushes hard-boiled yolks with mustard, mounts them with oil and folds in gherkins, capers, herbs and fine strips of the cooked whites, for cold fish and calf's head. Céleri rémoulade, the bistro salad, is raw celeriac cut into fine matchsticks in a sharp mustard mayonnaise.

The New Orleans rémoulade, taught as Creole rémoulade, kept the name and changed nearly everything: pink with paprika, hot with cayenne and horseradish, led by Creole mustard, sometimes with no mayonnaise at all. The French sauce is white, sharp and herby but never hot, led by its pickles and capers.

These sauces split as mayonnaise does, from oil added too fast or too cold. The rescue, a fresh yolk and patience, is taught with how emulsions break. Aïoli grows hotter and more bitter as it stands, so make it the day it is served. A rémoulade weeps when its gherkins and capers go in wet, and a gribiche turns grey and sulphurous when its eggs were boiled too long.

At Brennan's a chive rémoulade comes with the Crawfish Meat Pies, a snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list in the Roost Bar. The house guide calls it cool, tangy and herby against the hot pastry. The menu does not print the recipe, so whether it leans French, white and herby, or New Orleans, pink and hot, is the kitchen's to say.

Describe aïoli as a garlic mayonnaise made with olive oil, and the French rémoulade as a white, herby mayonnaise with capers and pickles, close to tartare sauce. Most of these sauces are built on egg yolk and oil, but the house recipe is the kitchen's, so send every allergen question to the kitchen and the service note.

ratios.label: French rémoulade, to 250 ml (1 cup) of mayonnaise

faults.cause: Oil added faster than the yolk could take it, or oil and bowl too cold.
faults.fix: Whisk the broken sauce drop by drop into a fresh yolk or a spoonful of warm water in a clean bowl.

faults.cause: Old garlic with its green shoot left in, strong extra virgin oil beaten in a blender, or a sauce made too far ahead.
faults.fix: Use fresh garlic with the shoot removed and part mild oil, and make it the day it is served.

faults.cause: Gherkins and capers added wet with their brine.
faults.fix: Squeeze them dry in a cloth before they go in.

faults.cause: The eggs were boiled too long and not cooled.
faults.fix: Boil them about 10 minutes and cool them at once in iced water.

cards.front: What is aïoli, at its simplest?
cards.back: Garlic pounded to a paste with salt, with olive oil worked in drop by drop; most kitchens add a yolk for a steadier sauce.

cards.front: What does the name aïoli mean?
cards.back: It joins the Provençal words for garlic and oil, which is all the oldest version holds.

cards.front: What is le grand aïoli?
cards.back: A Provençal meal built around a bowl of aïoli: poached salt cod, boiled vegetables and hard-boiled eggs, all dipped in the sauce.

cards.front: What is rouille, and what is it served with?
cards.back: Aïoli’s red cousin, with chilli, saffron and soaked bread; spread on toasts and floated on bouillabaisse, the fish stew of Marseille.

cards.front: What goes into a French rémoulade?
cards.back: Mayonnaise with mustard, chopped gherkins, capers, chopped herbs such as parsley, chervil and tarragon, and a little anchovy.

cards.front: How did the classical French tartare differ from an ordinary mayonnaise?
cards.back: It was mounted on hard-boiled yolks pounded smooth rather than raw ones, and finished with chives.

cards.front: How is a gribiche made?
cards.back: Hard-boiled yolks crushed with mustard and mounted with oil, then gherkins, capers, herbs and strips of the cooked whites folded in.

cards.front: What is céleri rémoulade?
cards.back: Raw celeriac cut into fine matchsticks and dressed in a sharp mustard mayonnaise: a French bistro salad named for the sauce.

cards.front: How does the French rémoulade differ from the New Orleans one?
cards.back: The French is white, sharp and herby but not hot, led by pickles and capers; the New Orleans is pink and hot, led by Creole mustard, paprika and horseradish.

cards.front: Why do many cooks avoid beating all strong extra virgin oil into aïoli in a blender?
cards.back: Hard beating can turn a peppery extra virgin oil bitter, so they use part mild olive oil or work by hand.

cards.front: Why squeeze gherkins and capers dry before they go into a rémoulade?
cards.back: Their brine thins the sauce and makes it weep; dry, they add crunch and sharpness without loosening it.

cards.front: Which Brennan’s dish carries a rémoulade, and which style is it?
cards.back: The Crawfish Meat Pies, with a chive rémoulade for dipping; the recipe is not printed, so the kitchen says which style it is.

questions.q: At its oldest, what is a Provençal aïoli made from?
questions.answer: Garlic, salt and olive oil
distractors: Garlic, egg yolk and lemon juice
questions.why: The oldest aïoli is garlic pounded with salt and mounted with olive oil; the yolk most kitchens add came later, for steadiness.

questions.q: What does the word aïoli join together?
questions.answer: The Provençal words for garlic and oil
distractors: The French words for egg and lemon
A cook’s name and a Provençal village
The Italian words for garlic and bread
questions.why: The name is the recipe: garlic and oil, the two things the oldest version of the sauce holds.

questions.q: Which sauce is spread on toasts and floated on bouillabaisse?
questions.answer: Rouille
questions.why: Rouille, red with chilli and saffron and thickened with bread, is the classic partner of the Marseille fish stew.

questions.q: Which additions turn mayonnaise into a French rémoulade?
questions.answer: Mustard, gherkins, capers, herbs and anchovy
distractors: Tomato paste, shallot and a tarragon reduction
questions.why: The French rémoulade is white and herby, built on pickles, capers, herbs and anchovy; paprika and horseradish belong to the New Orleans sauce.

questions.q: The classical French tartare was mounted on which kind of yolks?
questions.answer: Hard-boiled yolks, pounded smooth
distractors: Raw yolks warmed over simmering water
questions.why: The classical tartare pounded cooked yolks and mounted them with oil, finishing with chives; the modern one is usually a mayonnaise with pickles and capers.

questions.q: Besides gherkins, capers and herbs, what is folded into a gribiche at the end?
questions.answer: Fine strips of the cooked egg whites
questions.why: Gribiche is built on hard-boiled yolks, so the whites are cut into strips and folded back in for texture.

questions.q: Céleri rémoulade, the French bistro salad, is made from which vegetable?
questions.answer: Celeriac
questions.why: Raw celeriac, the knobbly root, is cut into fine matchsticks and dressed in a sharp mustard mayonnaise.

questions.q: A guest asks how the French rémoulade differs from the New Orleans one. What is the short, honest answer?
questions.answer: French is white and herby; New Orleans is pink and hot
distractors: They are the same sauce, sold under two different names
French is hot with cayenne; New Orleans is mild
French is made with butter; New Orleans with oil
questions.why: The New Orleans sauce kept the name but took paprika, cayenne, horseradish and Creole mustard; the French one stays white with pickles and herbs.

questions.q: Which Brennan’s dish comes with a chive rémoulade?
questions.answer: Crawfish Meat Pies
questions.why: The chive rémoulade is the dip for the Crawfish Meat Pies on the Bubbles list; the crab claws carry a brown butter vinaigrette.

entries.title: Vinaigrette
entries.summary: Vinaigrette is oil and vinegar whisked into a temporary emulsion, classically three parts oil to one of acid, with salt, mustard and shallot dissolved in the acid first. Warm versions of bacon fat or brown butter coat leaves better.
entries.guest: A vinaigrette is a dressing of oil and vinegar, whisked with mustard and shallot. Our Louisiana Crab Claws come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette, nutty and bright.

paras: A vinaigrette is one of the simplest sauces in the cold kitchen and one of the most used: oil and an acid, usually vinegar, seasoned and whisked so the oil breaks into tiny droplets through the vinegar. Left alone it separates within minutes, because nothing strong holds the droplets apart. That makes it a temporary emulsion, an emulsion being fat held in droplets through a watery liquid, and it is why a vinaigrette is whisked or shaken again just before use. A little mustard slows the parting: its fine particles and natural gums coat the droplets and keep the dressing creamy for longer.
The name comes from vinaigre, vinegar, which itself means sour wine. Beyond leaves, it dresses leeks, asparagus, boiled potatoes, lentils, grilled fish and cold meats.

The classic ratio is three parts oil to one of vinegar by volume: 180 ml (3/4 cup) of oil to 60 ml (1/4 cup) of vinegar dresses about eight salads. Put the vinegar in a bowl with a good pinch of salt, 1 tsp (5 ml) of Dijon mustard and 1 tbsp (15 ml) of finely chopped shallot, and leave it for five minutes. Salt dissolves in vinegar but not in oil, and the acid softens the shallot's raw bite. Whisk in the oil in a slow stream until the dressing thickens slightly and turns opaque, then add pepper.

Taste it on a leaf, not from a spoon: neat, every dressing tastes harsh, and the leaves soften it, so a dressing balanced on the spoon eats flat and oily on the salad. On its own it should taste a touch too sharp and salty. A sharp acid such as lemon juice may want four parts oil; a mellow Champagne or cane vinegar can take a little less.

Dress leaves at the last moment, in a wide bowl, with a little dressing, turning them until every leaf shines and nothing pools on the plate. The leaves must be dry, because water repels oil and thins the dressing, and acid and salt wilt tender leaves within minutes, so a dressed salad cannot wait. Potatoes, lentils and leeks are the exception: dressed warm, they drink it in.

The acid sets the character. Red wine vinegar is robust, for bitter leaves and beef; white wine vinegar is clean and does everything; sherry vinegar is nutty and deep, for walnuts, mushrooms and warm dressings; Champagne vinegar is light and delicate, for soft leaves and seafood; Louisiana cane vinegar, made from sugar cane, is mild with a soft sweetness; lemon juice is fresh but fades within hours.

Warm vinaigrettes swap some or all of the oil for a warm fat. Bacon fat, rendered from lardons (small batons of bacon) and sharpened with vinegar in the same pan, dresses the frisée, the curly, bitter endive, of a Lyonnaise salad. Brown butter is whisked with acid into a nutty dressing; brown butter itself is taught with beurre noisette. Warm dressings coat better because warm fat is thinner and flows into every fold of a leaf, and the warmth softens sturdy greens so they take the dressing in.

A dressing that separates was not whisked hard enough or has no mustard; whisk it again just before use. One that tastes harsh even on a leaf has too much acid, or salt stirred into the oil, where it never dissolves. A warm vinaigrette gone thick and cloudy has simply cooled, and butter and bacon fat set: warm it gently, whisk and serve at once.

At Brennan's the Louisiana Crab Claws come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette: butter browned until nutty, sharpened with acid so it is rich but bright, with fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, the classic French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, tossed through at the last moment. The house guide does not name the acid, so ask the kitchen before naming it to a guest.

Say vin-uh-GRET and describe it plainly as a dressing of oil and vinegar. For the claws, say warm brown butter vinaigrette, nutty and bright, and say warm aloud, because many guests expect cold claws. Questions about what is in any dressing, mustard or anything else, go to the kitchen and the service note.

faults.fix: Whisk or shake it again just before use; a spoonful of mustard holds it longer.

faults.cause: Too much acid, or salt added to the oil, where it never dissolves.
faults.fix: Add oil a little at a time, and dissolve the salt in the vinegar first next time.

faults.fault: Pooling on the plate, limp leaves
faults.cause: Too much dressing, wet leaves, or dressed too early.
faults.fix: Dry the leaves, dress them at the last moment, and start with less dressing.

faults.fault: Warm dressing gone thick and cloudy
faults.cause: The butter or bacon fat cooled and began to set.
faults.fix: Warm it gently and whisk, then serve at once.

cards.front: Why is a vinaigrette called a temporary emulsion?
cards.back: Nothing strong holds the oil droplets apart, so it separates within minutes and must be whisked or shaken again before use.

cards.front: What is the classic ratio of oil to vinegar?
cards.back: Three parts oil to one of vinegar by volume; a sharper acid such as lemon juice may want four parts oil.

cards.front: Why dissolve the salt in the vinegar before the oil goes in?
cards.back: Salt dissolves in vinegar but not in oil; stirred into the oil it stays gritty and the dressing tastes harsh in patches.

cards.front: What does mustard do in a vinaigrette?
cards.back: Its fine particles and natural gums coat the oil droplets, so the dressing stays creamy and holds together for longer.

cards.front: Why let chopped shallot sit in the vinegar first?
cards.back: The acid softens it and takes off its raw, harsh bite before the oil goes in.

cards.front: Which vinegar suits a delicate seafood salad, and which a warm, nutty dressing?
cards.back: Champagne vinegar is light and delicate for seafood; sherry vinegar is nutty and deep for warm dressings, walnuts and mushrooms.

cards.front: What is cane vinegar, and how does it taste?
cards.back: Vinegar made from fermented sugar cane, made in Louisiana among other places: mild, with a soft sweetness, so it dresses without sharp edges.

cards.front: Why does a warm vinaigrette coat leaves better than a cold one?
cards.back: Warm fat is thinner, so it flows into every fold of a leaf, and the warmth softens sturdy greens so they take it in.

cards.front: When and how should leaves be dressed?
cards.back: At the last moment, dry, with a little dressing, tossed until every leaf shines and nothing pools on the plate.

cards.front: Why taste a vinaigrette on a leaf rather than from a spoon?
cards.back: Neat from a spoon every dressing tastes harsh; the leaves dilute it, so the leaf shows how it will really eat.

cards.front: What is a warm bacon vinaigrette, and which salad is it classic on?
cards.back: Bacon fat rendered from lardons, small batons of bacon, sharpened with vinegar in the same pan and poured warm over the curly, bitter frisée of a Lyonnaise salad.

cards.front: Which vinaigrette comes on Brennan’s Louisiana Crab Claws?
cards.back: A warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid and finished with fines herbes; the claws are served warm and many guests expect them cold, so say so aloud.

questions.q: What is the classic proportion of oil to vinegar in a vinaigrette?
questions.answer: Three parts oil to one of vinegar
distractors: One part oil to three of vinegar
Ten parts oil to one of vinegar
questions.why: Three to one balances fat and acid on most leaves; a sharper acid such as lemon may want a little more oil.

questions.q: Why does the salt go into the vinegar before the oil?
questions.answer: Salt dissolves in vinegar but not in oil
distractors: Salt makes the oil thicken faster
Salt turns the chopped shallot sweet at once
questions.why: Salt needs water to dissolve; stirred into oil it stays as grains and the dressing tastes harsh and uneven.

questions.q: What does a spoonful of mustard add to the structure of a vinaigrette?
questions.answer: It holds the oil droplets apart for longer
distractors: It replaces the need for any vinegar
It sets the oil firm, like butter from the fridge
It cooks the raw shallot right through
questions.why: Mustard’s fine particles and natural gums coat the droplets, so the temporary emulsion holds creamy for longer.

questions.q: Why must a vinaigrette be whisked or shaken again just before use?
questions.answer: It is a temporary emulsion and soon separates
distractors: The vinegar evaporates if it is left out
The mustard sinks to the bottom and turns bitter
The oil goes rancid within a few minutes
questions.why: Nothing strong holds the oil droplets apart, so they pool again within minutes and need whisking back through the vinegar.

questions.q: Why does a warm brown butter or bacon vinaigrette cling to leaves better than a cold one?
questions.answer: Warm fat runs thinly into every fold
distractors: Heat turns the vinegar into a thick syrup
Warm fat carries far more salt than oil
Heat makes the leaves repel the water
questions.why: Warm fat is thinner and runs into every fold, and the warmth softens sturdy greens so they take the dressing in.

questions.q: A dressed salad sits limp in a pool of vinaigrette. What most likely went wrong?
questions.answer: Too much dressing, added too early
distractors: Not enough salt dissolved in the vinegar
The oil was too cold to pour
The shallot was cut too fine
questions.why: Leaves are dressed at the last moment with a little dressing; extra pools, and acid and salt wilt tender leaves within minutes.

questions.q: Which vinegar is nutty and deep, suited to warm dressings, walnuts and mushrooms?
questions.answer: Sherry vinegar
questions.why: Sherry vinegar is aged and nutty; Champagne vinegar is lighter and better kept for delicate leaves and seafood.

questions.q: How should a cook taste a vinaigrette before dressing a salad?
questions.answer: On a leaf of the salad
questions.why: Neat, a vinaigrette always tastes too sharp, and the leaves soften it; balance it on a spoon and the salad eats flat, so the leaf gives the true reading.

questions.q: Which classic salad is dressed with a warm vinaigrette of bacon fat and vinegar?
questions.answer: Lyonnaise salad of frisée and lardons
questions.why: The Lyonnaise salad pours warm bacon fat, sharpened with vinegar in the pan, over bitter frisée; the warmth softens the sturdy leaves so they take the dressing in.

questions.q: What is tossed through the warm brown butter vinaigrette on Brennan’s Louisiana Crab Claws at the last moment?
questions.answer: Fines herbes
questions.why: The guide finishes the claws’ brown butter vinaigrette with fines herbes, the French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, added fresh so the heat does not dull them.

entries.title: Mignonette
entries.say: min-yo-NET (meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard)
entries.summary: Mignonette is the raw oyster’s sauce: finely chopped shallot in red wine or Champagne vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. A spoonful lifts the oyster’s brine without drowning it; ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley.
entries.guest: Mignonette is the classic raw oyster sauce: shallot, cracked pepper and vinegar. Ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley, a gentle warmth on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

paras: Mignonette, said min-yo-NET, is the sauce of the raw bar: shallot chopped very fine and steeped in red wine or Champagne vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. A raw oyster tastes of salt and the sea; a few drops of sharp vinegar, sweet shallot and the warmth of pepper lift that brine and clean the palate between oysters. It is one of the simplest sauces a Commis will make, and one of the most exact, because it sits beside one of the most delicate things on the menu.

The name comes from the pepper. In French kitchens mignonnette, spelt with two n's, is the old name for peppercorns coarsely cracked rather than ground to dust, and the sauce is named after it. That is its first lesson: crack the pepper, never powder it.

Cut one large shallot, about 40 g (1.5 oz), into the finest brunoise you can manage, tiny even dice of 1 to 2 mm, so each spoonful carries sweet shallot without a crunch of raw onion. Put it in a small bowl with 120 ml (1/2 cup) of red wine vinegar or Champagne vinegar. Crack 1 tsp (5 ml) of black peppercorns coarsely in a mortar or under the base of a heavy pan and stir them in; ready-ground pepper turns the vinegar muddy. Salt is optional, because the oyster brings its own.

Cover it and chill it for at least 30 minutes, so the shallot softens and gives the vinegar its sweetness. Make it fresh each day: after a day or two the shallot goes soft and grey and the sauce tastes flat.

Red wine vinegar gives a robust, pink sauce; Champagne vinegar a paler, gentler one for the most delicate oysters. Variations add finely grated lemon or lime zest, cucumber cut as fine as the shallot for coolness, fresh or preserved chilli for warmth, or chopped parsley or chives. Each stays a seasoning: a few drops of sharp, clean flavour, not a salsa.

At a New Orleans oyster bar the raw oyster more often meets cocktail sauce and hot sauce. Many New Orleans oyster bars hand guests ketchup, horseradish, lemon and hot sauce to mix their own cocktail sauce. Mignonette is the French-leaning choice, lighter and sharper than either, and the one that lets the oyster taste most of itself.

A spoonful, not a flood. Poured over ahead of time, the acid starts to firm the oyster, and too much drowns the brine the guest came for. Coarsely cut shallot crunches and takes over; finely ground pepper muddies the vinegar; a batch made days ahead tastes tired. A fierce vinegar is better swapped for a gentler one than watered down.

At Brennan's the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, a dinner starter and the first course of the dinner tasting, are served raw on the half shell with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette and parsley. The Fresno is a red chilli about as hot as a jalapeño but fruitier; preserved, salted or pickled, and diluted in the vinegar, it reads as a gentle, fruity warmth rather than real heat, which is why the service note calls it mild. How the chilli is preserved, and which vinegar the kitchen uses, are questions for the chef. One of the ten courtyard turtles is named Mignonette.

Say min-yo-NET, as the house guide does; meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard. Describe it as shallot, cracked pepper and vinegar, and ours as made with preserved Fresno chilli for a gentle warmth. The house guide says the guest spoons it onto each oyster at the table; it is never poured over in advance, so set it beside the oysters and show a first-timer how little to use. These oysters are raw, so give the consumer advisory the service note asks for: raw oysters carry a risk of illness, above all for guests who are pregnant, immunocompromised or have liver disease. Send every question about raw seafood to the kitchen or the manager.

cards.front: What is a mignonette?
cards.back: The raw oyster’s sauce: finely chopped shallot steeped in red wine or Champagne vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper.

cards.front: Where does the sauce get its name?
cards.back: From the pepper: mignonnette is the old French kitchen name for coarsely cracked peppercorns, the ingredient the sauce is named after.

cards.front: How fine should the shallot be cut, and why?
cards.back: A very fine brunoise, tiny even dice of 1 to 2 mm, so each spoonful carries sweet shallot without a crunch of raw onion.

cards.front: Why crack the peppercorns rather than use ready-ground pepper?
cards.back: Cracked pepper gives clean bursts of warmth; finely ground pepper turns the vinegar muddy and dusty.

cards.front: How long should a mignonette rest, and how long does it keep?
cards.back: At least 30 minutes, covered and chilled, so the shallot softens and sweetens the vinegar; make it fresh each day.

cards.front: How much mignonette goes on a raw oyster?
cards.back: A few drops to half a teaspoon: enough to lift the brine, never enough to drown it.

cards.front: Why is mignonette spooned on at the table rather than poured over in advance?
cards.back: Its acid starts to firm the oyster, so the guest adds it just before eating, as the house guide says.

cards.front: What else sits beside raw oysters at a New Orleans oyster bar?
cards.back: Cocktail sauce, often stirred by the guest from ketchup, horseradish, lemon and Louisiana hot sauce.

cards.front: What is in the mignonette on Brennan’s Grand Isle Jewel oysters?
cards.back: Preserved Fresno chilli and parsley with the shallot, pepper and vinegar: a gentle, fruity warmth rather than real heat.

cards.front: How hot is the Fresno chilli in our mignonette?
cards.back: About as hot as a jalapeño but fruitier; preserved and diluted in vinegar it reads as a gentle warmth, which is why the service note calls it mild.

cards.front: How does the house guide say mignonette?
cards.back: The house guide writes min-yo-NET; meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard at the table.

cards.front: What does the service note ask a server to give with the raw Grand Isle Jewel oysters?
cards.back: The consumer advisory on raw oysters. Questions about raw seafood go to the kitchen or the manager; a server never answers them alone.

questions.q: Which three things make a classic mignonette?
questions.answer: Shallot, vinegar and cracked pepper
distractors: Egg yolk, Dijon mustard and olive oil
questions.why: Mignonette is shallot steeped in vinegar with cracked pepper; ketchup and horseradish make cocktail sauce instead.

questions.q: The name mignonette comes from which ingredient?
questions.answer: Coarsely cracked pepper
questions.why: Mignonnette is the old French kitchen word for coarsely cracked peppercorns, and the sauce is named after them.

questions.q: How should a guest meet the mignonette with raw oysters?
questions.answer: A few drops spooned on just before eating
distractors: Poured over every oyster in the kitchen
Stirred into the oyster liquor an hour ahead
Warmed and ladled over like a butter sauce
questions.why: The acid starts to firm the oyster, so the guest spoons a little on at the table rather than having it poured over in advance.

questions.q: Why do cooks crack peppercorns for mignonette rather than use fine ground pepper?
questions.answer: Fine ground pepper muddies the vinegar
distractors: Ground pepper has no heat at all
questions.why: Coarsely cracked pepper gives clean bursts of warmth and keeps the vinegar clear; the sauce is even named for it.

questions.q: How should the shallot for a mignonette be cut?
questions.answer: In a very fine brunoise, tiny even dice
distractors: In thick rings, left raw and crisp for bite
questions.why: Tiny even dice soften in the vinegar and carry sweetness in every spoonful without a crunch of raw onion.

questions.q: At a New Orleans oyster bar, guests often stir their own version of which sauce?
questions.answer: Cocktail sauce
questions.why: Many bars set out ketchup, horseradish, lemon and hot sauce so guests mix cocktail sauce to their taste.

questions.q: What gives the mignonette on Brennan’s Grand Isle Jewel oysters its gentle warmth?
questions.answer: Preserved Fresno chilli
questions.why: The house mignonette is made with preserved Fresno chilli and parsley; diluted in vinegar, the chilli reads as a gentle, fruity warmth.

questions.q: What does the service note tell a server to give with the raw Grand Isle Jewel oysters?
questions.answer: The consumer advisory on raw oysters
distractors: A side of cocktail sauce and lemon wedges
The story of the oyster farm
questions.why: The oysters are served raw, so the service note asks for the consumer advisory, and questions about raw seafood go to the kitchen or the manager.

entries.title: How emulsions hold, break and come back
entries.say: As it reads: how emulsions hold, break and come back.
entries.summary: An emulsion is fat held in tiny droplets through water, or water through fat, by an emulsifier such as yolk, butter’s milk proteins or mustard. Heat, cold and haste break it; warm water, a fresh yolk or cold butter usually brings it back.
entries.guest: Hollandaise, béarnaise and beurre blanc are warm butter sauces: butter whisked into warm egg yolk or a sharp wine reduction until silky. They are delicate, so each comes to the table just warm.

paras: An emulsion is two liquids that will not mix, fat and water, persuaded into one smooth sauce. One is broken into droplets far too small to see and scattered through the other. In mayonnaise, hollandaise and beurre blanc, fat is scattered through a little water, lemon juice or reduction: an oil-in-water emulsion. Butter itself is the other way round, droplets of water held in fat, a water-in-oil emulsion, which is why it feels greasy rather than wet.

Left alone, droplets of fat find each other and pool. What stops them is an emulsifier, a molecule with one end that likes water and one that likes fat, which coats each droplet like a skin. Egg yolk is the great one: its lecithin and proteins hold mayonnaise and hollandaise. In a butter sauce the milk proteins already in the butter do the work, which is why beurre blanc needs no yolk. Mustard helps too, which is why it steadies a vinaigrette.

Warm emulsions break three ways. Too hot, and a yolk sauce scrambles: past about 70°C (158°F) the yolk proteins set into tiny curds, while a butter sauce pushed well past its working window loses its hold and the butterfat oils out in a clear, greasy layer. Too cool, sinking towards body heat, and the butterfat begins to set, so the sauce thickens, dulls and splits if it is rewarmed in a hurry. Too much fat too fast, and the emulsifier cannot coat droplets as quickly as they arrive, so they run together.

Cold emulsions break for mirror reasons. Oil added too fast, above all at the start, swamps the yolk before it has made any droplets. Too much oil for the yolk crowds the droplets until there is too little water to hold them: the sauce turns stiff and glassy, then suddenly greasy and thin. A cold bowl or cold oil makes the oil thick and slow to break into droplets, and a greasy bowl adds fat before the yolk is ready. Ingredients at room temperature and a clean, dry bowl prevent most breaks.

Most broken emulsions come back if you rebuild them a droplet at a time. Watch for the warning: a sauce that tightens, turns glassy or shows a sheen of fat at the edge is close to breaking, and a spoonful of warm water whisked straight in usually saves it. For a sauce split into a greasy pool, put a teaspoon of warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream once it takes. The fresh base gives the fat somewhere to go.
For hollandaise, first whisk the fresh yolk with a spoonful of water over barely simmering water to a light ribbon; a raw, cold yolk leaves the sauce thin.

For a beurre blanc starting to oil out from heat, take it off the stove and whisk in a cube or two of cold butter: the cold lowers the temperature and the new butter brings fresh milk proteins. If it has fully separated, warm a spoonful of reduction or cream in a clean pan and whisk the broken sauce back in slowly.

Know when to stop. A hollandaise or béarnaise that has truly scrambled, with visible curds of cooked egg, does not come back: heat has cooked the yolk, and no whisking will uncook it. Start a new batch.

Every cook breaks a sauce; the good ones say so at once. On the line a broken sauce is a calm moment, not a crisis: tell the chef, keep it off the plate, and rescue it or start again. A sauce that looks oily or grainy at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, goes back to the cook, never to the guest.

For servers, this explains the house's warm sauces: the hollandaise on the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen, the béarnaise on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak and the beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique are all warm emulsions. The house guide's warning about hollandaise says it in a line: too hot and it scrambles, too cool and it splits.

ratios.label: Fresh base to rebuild a split sauce
ratios.value: 1 tsp (5 ml) warm water, or 1 fresh yolk, for each 250 ml (1 cup) of broken sauce

ratios.label: Cooling an overheated beurre blanc
ratios.value: 1 or 2 cubes of cold butter, 2 cm each, whisked in off the heat

temps.label: Above this yolk sauces begin to curdle
Much above this a beurre blanc risks oiling out

faults.cause: Oil added too fast, too much oil for the yolk, or cold oil and a cold bowl.
faults.fix: Whisk the broken sauce drop by drop into a fresh yolk or a teaspoon of warm water in a clean bowl.

faults.cause: Held too hot, so the emulsion loosened and the butterfat ran together.
faults.fix: Off the heat, whisk in a cube or two of cold butter; if fully split, whisk it slowly into warm reduction or cream.

faults.fault: Butter sauce set thick and dull
faults.cause: Allowed to cool until the butterfat began to set.
faults.fix: Warm it very gently while whisking; never blast it with heat.

faults.fault: Stiff, glassy sauce about to break
faults.cause: Too little water left for the fat it carries.
faults.fix: Whisk in a spoonful of warm water at once, before it splits.

faults.cause: The yolks overheated and set into curds.
faults.fix: If only just grainy, whisk in cold water off the heat and strain; if truly scrambled, start again.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: What is an emulsion, in kitchen terms?
cards.back: Two liquids that will not mix, fat and water, with one broken into tiny droplets and held through the other by an emulsifier.

cards.front: How do oil-in-water and water-in-oil emulsions differ? Give an example of each.
cards.back: Oil-in-water scatters fat through water, as in mayonnaise and hollandaise; water-in-oil scatters water through fat, as in butter itself.

cards.front: Name three emulsifiers a cook relies on.
cards.back: The lecithin and proteins in egg yolk, the milk proteins already in butter, and mustard, whose particles and gums coat the droplets.

cards.front: What happens when a warm emulsion gets too hot?
cards.back: A yolk sauce scrambles into grainy curds past about 70°C (158°F); a butter sauce loses its hold and oils out in a clear, greasy layer.

cards.front: What happens when a butter sauce gets too cool?
cards.back: The butterfat begins to set, so the sauce thickens and dulls, and it splits if it is rewarmed in a hurry rather than gently, while whisking.

cards.front: Why do cold emulsions such as mayonnaise break?
cards.back: Oil added too fast, too much oil for the yolk, or a cold bowl and cold oil that will not break into droplets.

cards.front: Why does too much oil for one yolk break a mayonnaise?
cards.back: The droplets crowd until too little water is left to go round; the sauce turns stiff and glassy, then suddenly greasy.

cards.front: What warns you that an emulsion is about to break?
cards.back: It tightens and turns glassy, or a sheen of fat appears at the edge; a spoonful of warm water whisked in then usually saves it.

cards.front: How do you rescue a split mayonnaise or hollandaise?
cards.back: Put a fresh yolk or a teaspoon of warm water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce in drop by drop, then in a thin stream. For a hollandaise, first whisk the yolk with a spoonful of water over gentle heat to a ribbon.

cards.front: How do you save a beurre blanc that is starting to oil out from heat?
cards.back: Take it off the stove and whisk in a cube or two of cold butter: the cold lowers the heat and the butter adds fresh milk proteins.

cards.front: When is a broken sauce beyond rescue?
cards.back: When a yolk sauce has truly scrambled into curds: heat has cooked the egg, and no whisking uncooks it. Start a new batch.

cards.front: What should a cook do the moment a sauce breaks on the line?
cards.back: Say so at once, keep it off the plate, set the broken batch aside and rescue it or start again; it is a lesson, not a crisis.

questions.q: Butter itself is which kind of emulsion?
questions.answer: Water held in droplets through fat
distractors: Fat held in droplets through water
Air held in bubbles through cream
Not an emulsion at all, but pure fat
questions.why: Butter is water held in fat, which is why it feels greasy rather than wet; mayonnaise and hollandaise are the other way round, fat held in water.

questions.q: In a mayonnaise, what coats each oil droplet so the droplets cannot merge?
questions.answer: Lecithin and proteins from the yolk
distractors: Fine particles of cracked black pepper
questions.why: Yolk lecithin and proteins have one end that likes water and one that likes fat, so they skin each droplet and hold the sauce.

questions.q: A hollandaise has turned grainy, with tiny specks through it. What has happened?
questions.answer: The yolk proteins have set into curds
distractors: The butter went in too fast
The lemon juice has soured the butter
The salt has drawn the fat out
questions.why: Past about 70°C (158°F) yolk proteins cook and set, so the smooth sauce turns into tiny curds.

questions.q: A beurre blanc left at the side of the stove has thickened and turned dull. Why?
questions.answer: The butterfat has begun to set
distractors: The shallot has soaked up the butter
The sauce has started to boil
questions.why: As a butter sauce cools towards body heat its fat starts to set, and it will split when warmed again unless warmed gently.

questions.q: Which mistake most often breaks a mayonnaise at the very start?
questions.answer: Adding the oil too fast
distractors: Using a yolk at room temperature
questions.why: At the start the yolk has made no droplets yet, so a rush of oil swamps it; the first oil goes in a few drops at a time.

questions.q: Why does too much oil for one yolk break a mayonnaise?
questions.answer: The water runs out
distractors: The yolk starts to cook in the oil
The oil turns bitter and sour
The salt can no longer dissolve
questions.why: The droplets crowd until the water runs out, so the sauce turns stiff and glassy, then suddenly greasy.

questions.q: To rebuild a split hollandaise on a fresh yolk, what is done to that yolk first?
questions.answer: Whisked with water to a light ribbon
distractors: Used raw and cold, straight from the fridge
Beaten with a spoonful of flour
questions.why: A raw, cold yolk leaves the rebuilt sauce thin; whisked with a spoonful of water over barely simmering water to a ribbon, it is ready to take the broken sauce.

questions.q: A beurre blanc is starting to oil out from too much heat. What do you do first?
questions.answer: Off the heat, whisk in cold butter
distractors: Turn the heat up to bind it
Add a yolk and bring it to a boil
Whisk in a spoonful of flour
questions.why: Cold butter lowers the temperature and brings fresh milk proteins, so the sauce can take hold again.

questions.q: Which broken sauce cannot be rescued and must be made again?
questions.answer: A hollandaise scrambled into curds
distractors: A mayonnaise split from fast oil
A beurre blanc set from cold
questions.why: Scrambled yolk is cooked egg and cannot be uncooked; the other three come back with warm water, a fresh yolk, gentle heat or a whisk.
